```{r}
#| label: LoadPackages
library(SciDataReportR)
```

# Synthetic review data

```{r}
#| label: CreateExampleData
set.seed(2024)
df_Example <- data.frame(
  ID = seq_len(200),
  MeasurementA = rnorm(200),
  History = factor(rep(c("Absent", "Present"), each = 100))
)
df_Example$MeasurementB <- df_Example$MeasurementA + rnorm(200, sd = 0.1)
df_Example$Response <- df_Example$History
df_Example$Response[1] <- "Present"
df_Example$MeasurementB[2] <- 8
attr(df_Example$MeasurementA, "label") <- "Measurement A"
attr(df_Example$MeasurementB, "label") <- "Measurement B"
attr(df_Example$History, "label") <- "Recorded history"
attr(df_Example$Response, "label") <- "Related response"
```

::: callout-note
These are simulated observations, with a rare categorical disagreement and a
numeric relationship deliberately disrupted. No data file or codebook is loaded.
In a real analysis, load data and codebook together and run `RevalueData()` first;
these functions use its attached labels without recoding the data again.
:::

# Sending a review to collaborators

If the goal is simply to hand someone the problems in their data,
`CreateDataAnomalyReport()` is the whole workflow in one call. It screens the
data, builds the review queue, and writes two files:

- a standalone HTML explorer, which opens in any browser with no R, no Quarto
  and no network connection, and
- an Excel workbook, which a collaborator works through issue by issue and
  sends back.

```r
review <- CreateDataAnomalyReport(
  df_Example,
  variables = c("MeasurementA", "MeasurementB", "History", "Response"),
  id_var = "ID",
  Title = "Cohort data review"
)
review$Files
```

Everything below is the same workflow in steps, for when you want to choose
methods, inspect results in the console, or build the queue yourself.
`CreateDataAnomalyReport()` adds no detection behaviour of its own; it calls
exactly the functions in the following sections. Once decisions come back,
`ImportAnomalyReviewDecisions()` copies them into the queue and
`SummarizeAnomalyDecisions()` reports what reviewers concluded. Nothing is ever
corrected automatically.

# Choosing a detector

`DetectDataAnomalies()` requires explicit variable names. Identifiers and strata
are retained for review, not added to the model. `stratify_by` fits completely
separate detectors; small groups are reported as unavailable, never pooled.

- `conditional` discovers subgroups and returns suspicious values with learned
  conditions. It supplies native flags, without general record scores.
- `isolation` scores unusual records using isolation forest.
- `local` compares density with neighboring records. Numeric inputs use scaled
  Euclidean distance; mixed inputs use Gower distance, requiring quadratic memory.
- `distance` uses robust Mahalanobis distances on numeric columns.
- `cellwise` returns DDC residuals and flags for individual numeric entries.

Backends are optional dependencies. Only install those used by requested methods:
`outliertree`, `isotree`, `dbscan` (and `cluster` for mixed inputs), `robustbase`,
and `cellWise`. The `dates` method uses base R. Integer codes stay numeric; convert categories explicitly.

```{r}
#| label: DetectRecordCombinations
#| echo: true
if (requireNamespace("outliertree", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("isotree", quietly = TRUE)) {
  anomalies <- DetectDataAnomalies(
    data = df_Example,
    variables = c("MeasurementA", "MeasurementB", "History", "Response"),
    id_var = "ID",
    methods = c("conditional", "isolation"),
    method_args = list(isolation = list(ntrees = 100)),
    seed = 2024
  )
  anomalies$Summary
}
```

# Dates and relationships between dates

Date and POSIXct inputs are supported directly. The default methods now include
`dates`, which requires no optional backend. It screens each selected date column
and all unique date pairs, within each stratum, without guessing their meaning
from column names. Pair intervals are **second minus first in selected-column
order**. Negative intervals are not automatically errors.

```{r}
#| label: DateReviewExample
#| echo: true
df_Dates <- data.frame(
  StudyID = seq_len(40),
  FirstVisit = as.Date("2020-01-01") + seq_len(40)
)
df_Dates$SecondVisit <- df_Dates$FirstVisit + 100
df_Dates$SecondVisit[1] <- df_Dates$FirstVisit[1] + 1000
date_anomalies <- DetectDataAnomalies(
  df_Dates, variables = names(df_Dates), id_var = "StudyID", methods = "dates"
)
dplyr::filter(date_anomalies$DateResults, Flag %in% TRUE)
```

`id_var` is retained for review and automatically removed from model features,
even when included in `variables`. Without an ID, original row references still
identify findings. Duplicate or missing IDs are diagnosed; dates are compared
within a row, never silently combined across participant records.

Date checks use outer Tukey fences (Q1 - 3 IQR, Q3 + 3 IQR) and require 20 observed
values by default. If the IQR is zero, they flag departures only when at least 95%
of observed values share a single value. Otherwise the check is unavailable.
These defaults are configurable with `method_args = list(dates =
list(min_observations = 20, iqr_multiplier = 3, majority_fraction = 0.95))`.

Use `date_pairs = matrix(c("FirstVisit", "SecondVisit"), ncol = 2)` to limit pairs;
a zero-row two-column matrix requests column checks only. More than 100 automatically
selected pairs warns, without dropping comparisons. Large pair sets increase both
computation and the number of opportunities for false alarms.

`DateResults` contains all checks, readable observed dates, signed intervals in
days, sample sizes, observed ranges, fences, flags, and evaluation status. Column
numeric values and fences are elapsed days from the per-column reference recorded
in `Metadata$DateConversions`; readable date fences are provided too. Pair values
are actual elapsed days (timestamps use seconds/86400, not calendar-day counting).
Mixed Date/timestamp pairs treat Date as UTC midnight.

Other methods use numeric local copies of dates, while `ReviewData` retains
original classes and time zones. Date-like strings are not parsed automatically.
A consistent but incorrect calendar pattern may escape these empirical checks;
there are no hard-coded birth/diagnosis/visit rules.

# Scores and flags

Larger scores mean more unusual observations. Scores retain their native scales;
compare ranks **within a method and stratum**, not scores between methods.
Score-only methods flag the top 1 percent of scores within each method and
stratum by default (`flag_percentile = 0.99`), so a screen always produces
candidates rather than an unclassified column of scores. A named cutoff takes
precedence, for example `thresholds = c(distance = 4)`, and
`flag_percentile = NULL` restores unflagged scores ordered by rank alone. Every
one of these is a review budget chosen for convenience, not an estimated
probability of entry error, and small strata can legitimately yield no flags. Conditional and DDC methods supply native flags;
`thresholds = c(cellwise = 4)` overrides DDC flags using absolute residuals.

Missing strata, insufficient data, or failed fits stay `unavailable`. A method
without applicable variable types is `not applicable`. Neither means normal.
Native missing-data handling is used for conditional, isolation, and DDC methods;
LOF and robust distance use complete rows. No automatic imputation occurs.

```{r}
#| label: DetectNumericInconsistency
#| echo: true
if (requireNamespace("robustbase", quietly = TRUE)) {
  numeric_anomalies <- DetectDataAnomalies(
    df_Example, c("MeasurementA", "MeasurementB"),
    id_var = "ID", methods = "distance"
  )
  head(numeric_anomalies$Results[order(numeric_anomalies$Results$Rank), ])
}
```

# Longitudinal review

```{r}
#| label: CreateVisitExamples
set.seed(2024)
df_Visits <- expand.grid(ID = seq_len(15), Time = c(0, 1, 3, 6))
df_Visits$Measurement <- df_Visits$Time + rnorm(60)
df_Visits$State <- factor(ifelse(df_Visits$ID == 1 & df_Visits$Time == 6,
                               "Changed", "Stable"))
df_Visits$Measurement[20] <- 20
attr(df_Visits$Measurement, "label") <- "Repeated measurement"
attr(df_Visits$State, "label") <- "Recorded state"
attr(df_Visits$Time, "label") <- "Elapsed months"
longitudinal <- DetectLongitudinalAnomalies(
  df_Visits, c("Measurement", "State"), "ID", "Time",
  methods = c("change", "transition")
)
longitudinal$Summary
```

Change scores describe consecutive observed values divided by actual elapsed time.
They need ten intervals from five participants and nonzero MAD. Both endpoints
are linked in `IntervalResults`; a suspicious interval cannot tell us which value
is wrong. Missing observations are bridged, and the gap remains visible.

Transition scores estimate `1 - P(current | previous)` after excluding **all**
transitions from the scored participant. They need ten reference transitions from
five other participants for that preceding category. Rare valid transitions can
therefore score highly. Visit gaps are displayed but do not condition this model.

Request `methods = "trajectory"` to fit an `nlme` linear-time random-intercept model
for each numeric variable. Optional `covariates` add fixed effects. Each eligible
participant needs three complete visits and each stratum needs ten eligible
participants. Absolute in-sample Pearson residuals are exploratory diagnostics;
a large anomaly can influence its own fitted trajectory. They are not held-out
prediction errors or prediction intervals. Model failures are retained in diagnostics.

# Reviewing results

`Results` has one row per original record and method. `CellResults` locates numeric
or conditional evidence; `IntervalResults` links visit pairs. `ParticipantSummary`
counts distinct reviewed records and methods with flags, without double-counting
cells. `Diagnostics` explains excluded variables, missing labels, and skipped fits.
`Metadata` records settings and provenance. `ReviewData` preserves selected original
columns and `.Row` references without altering the input.

```{r}
#| label: ExploreVisitAnomalies
#| echo: true
if (requireNamespace("DT", quietly = TRUE)) {
  ExploreDataAnomalies(longitudinal, TopN = 2)
}
```

The explorer keeps full scrollable tables. Select rows to inspect original
values; details are generated only on selection.
The record grid searches scores and context, not source values inside details.
Set `IncludePlots = TRUE` to enable interactive figures on selection, or call
`PlotDataAnomalyTrajectories()` separately for selected participants. Compare
highlighted records against complete histories. Unusual biology, rare subgroups, batch effects, and errors
can all produce flags. Review source records before making any corrections.
Nothing is automatically corrected, removed, or saved.

# Collaborator decisions in Excel

The explorer now starts with an issue worklist. It converts detection results
using `CreateAnomalyReviewQueue()` and preserves the original technical tables
underneath. Study IDs are optional. Without one, source rows identify records
**within this detection snapshot**, not across reordered or revised datasets.

```{r}
#| label: CreateCollaboratorQueue
#| echo: true
review_queue <- CreateAnomalyReviewQueue(date_anomalies)
review_queue$Issues
```

By default, native flags, explicit cutoffs and the default percentile cutoff all
enter the queue.
`include_ranked = TRUE, top_n = 10` adds up to ten unclassified finite-scored
records per method and stratum, labeled exploratory. It does not identify an
incorrect field. `Priority` starts as `Unassigned` and is set by reviewers;
method scores are not averaged into an error probability.

If an ID was not passed to detection but is retained in `ReviewData`, add it
without refitting using `CreateAnomalyReviewQueue(result, id_var = "StudyID")`.
Missing and duplicate IDs remain separate source rows. Additional
`context_vars` must name retained columns; time and strata are included automatically.

For several clinical groups, use a named list:

```r
queue <- CreateAnomalyReviewQueue(
  list(BodyComposition = body_result, Metabolic = metabolic_result)
)
ExploreDataAnomalies(queue)
```

The analyses retain independent row namespaces. Evidence is consolidated only
within the same analysis, source row(s), and affected field set. Distinct date
pairs stay distinct. Multiple methods flagging an issue are not independent
confirmation. Conditional detection currently exposes at most one finding per
record, so a broadly flagged dataset is not an estimated error rate.

### Screening everything, reviewing a subset

Narrow what gets *listed* without narrowing what gets *modelled*. Pass the
columns you want to work through to `variables`:

```r
queue <- CreateAnomalyReviewQueue(anomalies, variables = c("BMI", "Weight"))
ExploreDataAnomalies(anomalies, variables = c("BMI", "Weight"))
CreateDataAnomalyReport(df_Data, review_variables = c("BMI", "Weight"))
```

Detection is unaffected: the models were fitted on the full selection, so a
listed finding is still conditioned on every screened column, and the coverage
summary still describes the whole screen. This is the reason to filter here
rather than restricting `variables` in `DetectDataAnomalies()`, which removes
the other columns from the comparison groups and changes the findings
themselves. Findings with no attributed field concern a whole record and are
always listed. Naming a column that was not screened is an error. In
`CreateDataAnomalyReport()`, `review_variables` filters the HTML explorer only;
the Excel workbook stays the complete record of findings.

Export only when ready, to a location outside the package:

```r
ExportAnomalyReviewQueue(queue, here::here("review", "AnomalyReview.xlsx"))
# Optional: keep the exact queue for a later R session.
# saveRDS(queue, here::here("review", "AnomalyReviewQueue.rds"))
```

The destination directory must already exist. By default the workbook is a
single **Review** sheet: one line per finding, about seventeen columns, no
wrapped paragraphs, built to be scanned and filled in. The long explanations,
the **Evidence** and **Read me** sheets and the snapshot manifest are not
written, which also makes the file an order of magnitude smaller.

That default cannot be read back into R. If collaborator decisions need to
return to the queue through `ImportAnomalyReviewDecisions()`, export with
`layout = "full"`, which writes every sheet and column as before:

```r
ExportAnomalyReviewQueue(queue, "AnomalyReview.xlsx", layout = "full")
``` Yellow review columns
are editable; original values remain unchanged. Status choices are `Unreviewed`,
`Confirmed correct`, `Correction needed`, and `Definition clarification`.
Priority choices are `Unassigned`, `High`, `Medium`, and `Low`. Use
`ProposedCorrection` for free-text proposed changes, and `SourceChecked`,
`Reviewer`, `ReviewedOn` (YYYY-MM-DD), and `Notes` for the review trail.

After collaborators edit the workbook:

```r
queue <- ImportAnomalyReviewDecisions(
  queue, here::here("review", "AnomalyReview.xlsx")
)
ExploreDataAnomalies(queue)
```

Blank imported reviewer fields leave existing decisions unchanged. An explicit
`Unreviewed` resets status. A workbook may return a subset of issue rows; omitted
issues keep their decisions. Keep all headers, the full Evidence sheet, and the
hidden manifest intact. Sorting is allowed. Changed findings, duplicate or unknown
issue IDs, and snapshot mismatches are rejected. Changed or reordered source data
require a new detection snapshot, even if participant IDs remain the same.

## Reading potential data issues

Tables scroll inside a 500-pixel panel instead of using page buttons. Search and
column filters operate across every retained row. Labels appear above variable
names, so collaborators can find the corresponding dataframe column. Select a
row to read its full evidence below the table. `TopN` is retained for compatibility
with earlier previews; interactive figures are selected individually.

**Conditional pattern** means an unusual value within a learned subgroup, or
within the whole column when no conditions were learned. The explanation names
the recorded value, direction or uncommon response, learned conditions, and
available reference statistics. These comparisons describe this dataset; they
are not clinical normal ranges or proof of an error. Older results without
structured statistics retain their original explanation.

```r
ExploreDataAnomalies(queue, TableHeight = 500, IncludePlots = TRUE)
```

With optional `plotly` installed, selecting an issue draws an interactive
numeric/date distribution, categorical frequency plot, signed date-interval
distribution, or complete retained numeric participant history. Hover for values,
drag to zoom, and double-click to reset. Red marks identify the reviewed value or
endpoints. Conditional plots use supported learned conditions when available;
the caption identifies the displayed population and any difference from the
backend reference sample. Plots are generated on selection using local
JavaScript; no external service receives data. `IncludePlots = FALSE` keeps the
HTML smaller. Record-only findings without an affected variable have no invented
field plot.

Excel includes the same **Why flagged** and **Comparison details**, with original
backend explanations retained separately. Variable keys are visible beside
labels. Existing matching workbooks remain importable; display formatting does
not change queue fingerprints or reviewer decisions.

The source dataframe is never updated automatically. Confirm corrections and
apply them through a separate, auditable cleaning workflow.

```{r}
#| label: Reproducibility
#| include: false
# save.image(here::here("DataAnomalyExamples.RData"))
print(sessionInfo())
```


`DetectDataAnomalies(df_Raw)` selects all supported columns without requiring
`RevalueData()`. Supply `id_var` and `stratify_by` to keep those columns out of
model inputs. Without a codebook, labels fall back to column names. Integer
codes remain numeric; raw character dates must be parsed as Date/POSIXct first.
List and other unsupported columns are reported and skipped only during automatic
selection; explicit unsupported selections error.

Plots now default on when `plotly` is installed, and the first issue is selected.
Use `IncludePlots = FALSE` to disable them. Print output contains the complete
static issue queue, independently of the current scroll position. Rare coded
values have their own explorer review category without changing detection flags.

## Suggested review order and exploratory combinations

`CreateAnomalyReviewQueue()` now includes up to ten unclassified scored records
per analysis, method and stratum by default. Use `include_ranked = FALSE` for a
flag-only queue, or `top_n` to change the number of exploratory records. These
candidates have no invented flag or affected field. Existing queue objects retain
their membership and decisions; rebuilding creates a new queue and does not
transfer previous decisions automatically.

The explorer and Excel derive suggested order without refitting. Scores are not
comparable across methods -- a missingness observed fraction and a conditional
boundary distance measure different things, and several methods emit native flags
with no record score at all -- so the order is driven by the kind of finding:
values inconsistent with related fields, then implausible dates and intervals,
conditional outliers, distribution outliers, changes and transitions, unexpected
missingness, rare numeric codes confined to -1/0/1, and finally exploratory record
combinations. Within a kind, findings with thin reference support (fewer than 20
comparable records) sort after better-supported ones, then available
within-method/stratum score percentiles (descending), reference counts and
deterministic issue IDs. Ties use midpoint empirical
percentiles; missing scores stay unavailable. The strongest supporting evidence
sets the position; repeated evidence does not increase priority. This is an
unvalidated review aid, not estimated error probability or clinical urgency.

For exploratory combinations, use the comparison X/Y selectors to inspect the
selected record against its stratum. The default axes use positive column-screening results when available, otherwise
the first two usable numeric model inputs. Other selections offer distributions or categorical counts.
These are descriptive comparisons, not isolation-forest feature attributions.
Raw scores, method ranks and original evidence remain under Technical details.

## Which columns are worth checking in an isolation record?

Column screening happens during detection while the fitted model is available.
No model is refit or saved. The default uses fast, batched single-column
replacements rather than expensive Monte Carlo SHAP:

```r
anomalies <- DetectDataAnomalies(
  df_Raw,
  explanation_args = list(top_n = 10, background_n = 50,
                          replacements = 3, batch_size = 64)
)
ExploreDataAnomalies(anomalies)
```

Study ID remains optional. `digest` is required for explanation fingerprints;
`fastshap` is only required for explicit SHAP runs. Set
`explain_isolation = FALSE` to skip all column explanations.
`explanation_args = list(rows = c(1, 23))` selects original source rows instead
of the ten highest-scoring records per stratum. Every actual model input is
screened, using its actual factor levels and date transformations; excluded
constants stay excluded. Original values remain unchanged.

The same three reproducibly sampled reference records are used for all columns
and selected records within a stratum, drawn from a background of up to 50
eligible records. Increase `replacements` for a broader replacement screen at
additional cost. `batch_size` controls prediction batches and is automatically
reduced for very wide inputs.

`FeatureSensitivity` reports **score decrease = original isolation score minus
mean score after replacing one column**. Positive means that replacing this
column reduced the anomaly score; negative means it increased the score. These
are inspection leads, not identified errors or replacement recommendations.
Effects are not additive. Replacement-score ranges describe only the sampled
replacements, not confidence intervals or probabilities of error. Reference
records can contain errors, and replacing correlated/derived values can create
unrealistic combinations.

The selected-finding panel shows **Columns worth checking**, an interactive
signed-effect chart, five positive and five negative effects initially, and an
expandable complete table. Comparison plots start with leading positive effects.
If none are positive, no problem columns are inferred. Conditional/date/cell
findings are linked separately as additional evidence, not confirmation.

For slower additive SHAP explanations, request them explicitly:

```r
anomalies_shap <- DetectDataAnomalies(
  df_Raw,
  explanation_args = list(method = "shap", rows = c(1, 23),
                          background_n = 50, nsim = 64, repeats = 3)
)
```

This requires `fastshap >= 0.1.1` and can be expensive for wide datasets.
`nsim` and `repeats` apply only to SHAP; `replacements` and `batch_size` apply
only to sensitivity screening. `FeatureContributions` remains exclusively SHAP:
mean signed additive contributions, Monte Carlo SD/range and positive ranks.
Positive contributions raise the score relative to the background; negative
ones lower it. Monte Carlo variability is not confidence that a value is wrong.
The explorer retains the SHAP contribution waterfall for these results.

`ExplanationSummary` identifies the method and distinguishes **Explained**,
**Not requested**, and **Unavailable** records. Baseline and additive reconstruction
fields are unavailable for sensitivity. Failures preserve successful detection
scores. `ExplanationMetadata` records backgrounds, replacement reference rows,
seeds, inputs, transformations, elapsed screening time and a separate fingerprint.
Elapsed time is excluded from the fingerprint. Neither explanation method changes
flags, suggested review order, human priority, issue identity or queue snapshots.

Excel retains the original workflow and its **Contributions** sheet, with explicit
explanation-method labels and the appropriate screening or SHAP fields. Explanation
evidence is separately validated on import; matching older four-sheet workbooks
remain supported. Old saved results retain their explanations and decisions;
the explorer never silently refits or computes explanations.

## Review by codebook category

Pass a codebook when detecting anomalies to retain labels and categories for the
explorer and Excel. Matching uses raw variable names in `Variable`; `Label` and
`Category` are optional. Study ID is still optional.

```r
anomalies <- DetectDataAnomalies(df_All, codebook = VariableTypes)
ExploreDataAnomalies(anomalies)
queue <- CreateAnomalyReviewQueue(anomalies)
# ExportAnomalyReviewQueue(queue, "AnomalyReview.xlsx")
```

Labels and categories supply presentation metadata. Explicit temporal declarations
(`Type = "clock"` or `"duration"`, with `TimeUnit`/`TimeFormat`) also control local
modeling transformations. Other codebook types do not trigger conversion or value
recoding during detection, and detection does not call `RevalueData()`. Use `RevalueData()` separately beforehand when recoding is wanted.
Explicit nonblank codebook labels take precedence over attached labels, then
variable names. `Relabel = FALSE` keeps raw names; category filtering still works.
Missing categories appear as **Uncategorized**. Diagnostics identify unmatched
retained variables, unused codebook entries and missing labels/categories.
Identical duplicate entries collapse; conflicting entries for a variable error.

Existing detection results can receive a codebook without running detection again:

```r
queue <- CreateAnomalyReviewQueue(anomalies, codebook = VariableTypes)
ExploreDataAnomalies(queue)
# Or apply a temporary override just to this explorer:
ExploreDataAnomalies(anomalies, codebook = VariableTypes)
```

A queue-level codebook persists for subsequent Excel exports. An explorer-only
override affects that view. Each analysis otherwise keeps its own saved catalog;
a supplied common codebook overrides matching names across analyses.

Giving the codebook once to `DetectDataAnomalies()` is enough for everything
downstream: the queue, the saved explorer and the Excel workbook all read the
resolved catalog stored on the result, so `codebook` need not be repeated. It is
also the only place where codebook `Type` declarations can change what is
modelled -- a codebook supplied to a review view cannot alter models already
fitted, and records a `temporal_declarations_not_applied` diagnostic saying so.
The compact workbook carries a **Codebook category** column when a codebook
assigned a category to at least one screened column, and omits it otherwise
rather than filling it with `Uncategorized`.

Both tables carry a dropdown per categorical column: extreme value, anomaly
type, severity tier, codebook category, method, and analysis group where there
is more than one. A column with fewer than two distinct values is omitted.

**Extreme value** marks a record sitting at least ten times further from its
column median than any other record does, and those findings are listed ahead of
every tier: the kind of finding is the same whether a value is slightly or
absurdly out of range, so severity alone can sort an obvious data-entry error
behind dozens of findings that need judgement. The test is scale free, needs at
least ten other numeric values in the column, and is not applied to dates, clock
times or blanks.

**Anomaly type** describes the kind of finding, and **Severity tier** ranks those
kinds: tier 1 is a value that contradicts related fields in the same record, tier 8
an exploratory whole-record combination. Both are sortable columns on both tables,
and the tier is what the suggested review order follows, because scores from
different methods are not comparable. The page defines every tier and the types in
it. Above the tables, the **anomaly map** draws one cell per modelled variable and
record: grey where no anomaly was reported, coloured by kind otherwise, with the
record, the recorded value and the reason on hover. A cell carrying several
findings takes the most serious one, and findings with no attributed field are
counted beneath the map rather than placed on it.

**Codebook category** describes the
fields involved. A date pair can belong to both dates' categories and appears
when either category is selected. Category filtering uses exact membership,
including names containing punctuation or overlapping category names.

For isolation records, **Suggested inspection categories** come from the five
largest positive replacement-screening effects, or saved SHAP contributions.
The selected panel lists the supplying columns. These are inspection leads,
not identified incorrect fields. Without usable positive effects the category
is **Whole record—category unspecified**. Categories of conditional comparison
variables appear separately from the affected field's category.

The main **Potential data issues** queue omits review decisions because it is
read-only. Edit decisions in Excel, import them, and view them in selected-finding
details. Variable-level evidence means evidence about specific row–column values;
it supports the issue queue rather than independently confirming an error, and it
stays on the result object and in the Excel workbook rather than on the shared page.
**What the methods mean** describes all available detectors and anomaly types,
with requested methods first. Methods, supporting evidence and isolation column
screening are different parts of review; none estimates entry-error probability.

## Clock times and elapsed durations

An `hms` column can represent a clock or an elapsed task duration; its storage
class cannot establish that meaning. Declare it explicitly in codebook `Type`
as `clock` or `duration` (case-insensitive). Plain `difftime` defaults to duration
in detection; unclassified `hms` produces an actionable declaration request.

For the four columns discussed here, the supplied mapping is:

```r
vars_Clock <- c("tox_time", "gna_starttime")
vars_Duration <- c("gp_dom_time", "gp_nondom_time")
# QUESTION: The two clock classifications are provisional; confirm their definitions.
VariableTypes <- VariableTypes %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Type = dplyr::case_when(
    Variable %in% vars_Clock ~ "clock",
    Variable %in% vars_Duration ~ "duration",
    TRUE ~ Type
  ))

df_Revalued <- RevalueData(
  COVID_Database_2026_09_26_09_AM,
  codebook = VariableTypes
)$RevaluedData

d <- DetectDataAnomalies(
  df_Revalued,
  variables = names(df_Revalued)[1:400],
  codebook = VariableTypes
)
ExploreDataAnomalies(d)
```

Use names from the same dataframe passed to detection. No temporal meaning is
inferred from the spelling of these names. The codebook file is never written
back automatically.

Existing `hms`/`difftime` inputs retain their physical values, classes and unit
attributes in `RevalueData()`; the output gains `scidr_type` metadata.
`TimeMetadata` records declarations, provenance, conversion status and errors.
For numeric inputs declare `TimeUnit`: `secs`, `mins`, `hours`, `days` or `weeks`
(usual aliases such as seconds/minutes are accepted). Typed objects use their
own units. Text requires an explicit `TimeFormat`: `HMS`, `HM` or `MS`;
clock text supports `HMS`/`HM`, while durations support all three. Fractional
seconds and durations longer than one day are supported. Two-part text is never
guessed. Numeric HHMM codes are not guessed either.

```r
# Explicit numeric/text intake, with labels still supplied by your codebook:
result <- RevalueData(
  df_Raw,
  codebook = VariableTypes,
  time_types = c(assessment_clock = "clock", task_duration = "duration"),
  time_units = c(task_duration = "mins"),
  time_formats = c(assessment_clock = "HMS")
)
```

The same three named overrides are accepted by `DetectDataAnomalies()` for raw
inputs. Explicit overrides take precedence over temporal codebook declarations,
then attached temporal metadata. The detector transforms only local copies;
its `ReviewData` preserves original inputs and classes. Explorer-only codebook
overrides remain presentation choices and never refit or reinterpret saved models.

Missing codes are processed before temporal parsing in intake. Invalid components
are not rolled over. Clock values must lie in `[00:00, 24:00)`; negative/long
durations can be valid. Default intake errors name the variable and rows;
`on_error = "warn"` leaves a failed column unchanged and records the error.
Categorical value-code mappings conflict with a declared temporal conversion.
Optional `hms` is needed only when creating a clock object.

Detection converts durations to seconds and clock times to paired sine/cosine
coordinates on a 24-hour circle. Thus 23:59 and 00:01 are close. Clock pairs use
joint scaling for numeric LOF and circular distance for mixed-data LOF.
Conditional findings describe clock regions rather than high/low component
values. Cellwise clock findings retain native component evidence without
inventing an expected replacement time. Backend support requirements remain in
force; failures do not trigger another algorithm.

Fast column screening replaces an entire clock field with a reference value,
updating both coordinates together. Optional SHAP explains original fields
through the exact encoded prediction wrapper, preserving score reconstruction.
Neither displays two clock coordinates as independent evidence. Clock plots use
24-hour circular distributions; their half-hour display bins are not detection
thresholds. Duration displays identify their units explicitly.

`Metadata$TimeConversions` and `Metadata$FeatureMaps` record temporal processing,
including excluded components. Invalid clock values remain in the source and are
diagnosed, not wrapped to another time. Unparseable text is unavailable for the
affected field/row; other valid rows are retained. Missing parsing configuration
makes that temporal column unavailable. Native missing-data handling still applies.

Clock-only columns do not enter `date_pairs` and cannot establish elapsed time
between events on unknown days. Calendar dates/timestamps keep their existing
handling. Circular longitudinal trajectories and extracting a clock by silently
stripping a calendar date are outside this release. Older snapshots/workbooks
remain usable; adding new temporal modeling requires a new detection run.


## Review variables and unexpected missingness

`ExploreDataAnomalies()` starts with **Variables to review**. Select a variable
(label and raw name are shown) to filter the individual findings. **Show all
findings** resets that selection. Ranking uses the strongest supported finding;
it is not a probability that the variable contains an error. Findings with no
attributed field share the same table; filter by **Anomaly type** to list them on
their own, remembering that isolation screening supplies leads, not attributed errors.
Miniature distributions show retained values in the same stratum, with review
values highlighted in red. Detailed plots retain the actual comparison context.

Unexpected missingness is screened automatically, and "unexpected" is judged
against the rest of the record rather than against the column as a whole. A blank
is reported only when something in the data explains why it is unexpected, and
there are exactly two such explanations.

The first is a **rule learned from another column's values**. A small tree learns
which records are expected to carry a value, so a field collected from only part
of the sample — menopause status, say — is not reported for the records that
legitimately skip it, while a blank among the records that should have one is.
The finding reads "Blank, although 142 of 142 records with Sex = Female have a
value"; expand it to inspect the full learned condition.

The second is a **group of variables that go missing together**. Wide analysis
frames are usually merges of separate forms, and a form that was not done leaves
every one of its fields blank at once. That co-absence is discoverable: columns
are clustered on how similarly they go blank, which recovers the forms without
knowing what any column measures. A record carrying most of a group but not all
of it, where nearly everyone carrying any of that group carries all of it, is a
finding, and it names the pattern it used:

> Blank, although this record has 7 of the 8 variables in a group that go
> missing together (WBC, RBC, Hgb, Hct, MCV, Plt, Neut%, Lymph%), and 108 of the
> 112 records carrying any of that group have all 8.

This is why a column's overall completeness is not a gate. A panel only 40% of
the cohort completed is still screened, because the comparison group is the
records who did that panel, not everybody. A record missing *most* of a group has
skipped the form and is not reported.

A blank that neither mechanism explains is **not reported at all**. There is no
comparison group for it, and "this column is mostly full and you are blank" is a
fact about the column rather than an anomaly about the record; such columns are
listed in the explorer's **Completeness** section with their blank counts
instead. The discovered groups are listed in their own section on the page and
returned in `Metadata$Settings$missingness$Blocks` — check the membership before
trusting what the findings say, and raise `block_similarity` if a group has
merged variables from unrelated forms. An over-merged group is largely
self-limiting, since it rarely reaches the completion rate needed to report
anything.

The evaluated participant is excluded when an ID is available; otherwise the
evaluated row is excluded. Legitimate skip logic, selective testing, and study
design can still explain a blank.

```{r}
#| label: MissingnessScreeningExample
#| eval: false

d <- DetectDataAnomalies(
  df_Revalued,
  codebook = VariableTypes,
  method_args = list(missingness = list(
    min_reference = 20,
    min_observed_fraction = 0.95,
    maxdepth = 4
  ))
)
ExploreDataAnomalies(d)

# Run only missingness screening, using the same result/explorer workflow.
d_Missing <- DetectDataAnomalies(df_Revalued, methods = "missingness")

# Keep the previous set of detectors without missingness screening.
d_Values <- DetectDataAnomalies(
  df_Revalued,
  methods = c("conditional", "isolation", "dates")
)
```

The screening uses `is.na()` as supplied. It does not reinterpret sentinel codes,
change values, or impute blanks. Numeric/date/duration groups use quartiles by
default; clock groups use four six-hour regions; categorical value groups are
limited to 20 levels. Presence/absence groups remain available for high-cardinality
fields. Supported reference groups need at least 20 records and 95% observed
values by default. These are descriptive screening choices across many comparisons,
not calibrated confidence levels. All-missing variables and insufficient support
are reported without inventing an expected value. Existing results can use the
new presentation without refitting, but generating missingness evidence requires
running detection again.
